stories.text: The first Albert Hall, a temperance hall by Watson Fothergill, opened in 1876 and from 1902 was a Wesleyan Methodist mission; it burnt down on 22 April 1906. Albert Edward Lambert designed the present hall, dedicated in 1909, and it stayed a Methodist mission until 1982. It is now a conference and concert venue.

Helen Watts, the daughter of the vicar of Lenton, joined Nottingham's suffragettes after hearing Christabel Pankhurst speak in 1907. In 1909 she served a month in Holloway, was arrested here at the Albert Hall in July and let go without charge, and went on hunger strike in Leicester gaol.

stories.text: A Georgian town house was built here in 1752. The Nottingham Subscription Library, founded in 1816, moved in during 1821. In 1836 a meridian line was laid so that the library's longcase clock could keep Nottingham time, 4 minutes and 33 seconds behind Greenwich, and it still does. In 1841 Alfred Barber opened the first photographic studio in the Midlands in its attics.
Edith Ransom (1872–1949) was the first woman president of Bromley House Library.
Ellen Harrington was the first woman librarian of Bromley House, from 1943 to 1983. Her portrait hangs here, in a room named after her.
George Green, the mathematician, was a miller: his family's windmill in Sneinton is restored and named after him.[^s1] He was a member of the subscription library at Bromley House.[^s1][^s2]

stories.text: A legacy from the banker John Key paid for a hospital on part of Nottingham Park. Its first building, designed by John Simpson, was begun on 12 February 1781 and opened with 44 beds in September 1782; John Wesley was an early visitor. In 1844 it took in the hurt when a stand collapsed at a hanging on Garner's Hill, killing twelve. Hine added a storey in 1855, and Alfred Waterhouse's round Jubilee Wing opened in 1900. It closed in 1992, its work moved to the Queen's Medical Centre.
